unsupported.text: Europe’s crypto regulatory landscape has shifted from fragmented national registration regimes to a dense, layered system combining market licensing, stablecoin rules, anti-money laundering controls, transfer-data obligations, operational resilience, and—in some cases—payment-services regulation. The most consequential changes are not only MiCA’s entry into force, but also the end of grandfathering on 1 July 2026, the immediate enforceability of the EU Travel Rule from 30 December 2024, ESMA’s restrictive approach to reverse solicitation, the application of DORA from 17 January 2025, and the EBA’s view that some e-money token (EMT) activities can trigger PSD2. Taken together, these changes materially raise the compliance threshold for exchanges, custodians, brokers, wallet providers, stablecoin businesses, and non-EU firms serving EU users. This report argues that Europe is no longer merely “regulating crypto”; it is integrating crypto into mainstream financial regulation. The result is a more credible but also more demanding market structure that advantages authorised, well-capitalised operators and sharply reduces the viability of informal or offshore EU-facing business models. (InnReg, 2026; ESMA, 2026a; EBA, 2025)

The key regulatory change affecting the European crypto industry is that Europe now applies a multi-layered financial-regulation model to crypto rather than a standalone crypto rulebook. MiCA governs crypto-asset issuers and crypto-asset service providers (CASPs), the Transfer of Funds Regulation (TFR) imposes the EU crypto Travel Rule, AML laws continue to supply customer due diligence and suspicious activity reporting duties, DORA imposes operational resilience rules, and PSD2 can apply where crypto products—especially EMT-related payment flows—function like payment services. This regime applies not only to EU-incorporated firms but also to non-EU firms that target or serve EU users. (InnReg, 2026)

MiCA did not simply create a new licence. It also ended the prior world in which many firms operated under divergent national virtual-asset or AML-only registration regimes. The transitional regime under Article 143(3) was available only to CASPs that were already lawfully operating under national law before 30 December 2024, and even then only until the earlier of their national deadline, 1 July 2026, or the date their MiCA application was granted or refused. (Deloitte Legal, n.d.; Sumsub, n.d.)

ESMA’s 17 April 2026 statement removed any remaining ambiguity: after 1 July 2026, entities providing crypto-asset services to EU clients without a MiCA licence are in breach of EU law, regardless of how far local implementation had progressed in any given Member State. ESMA also expected unauthorised firms to have operational, credible, immediately executable wind-down plans already in place by that date. (ESMA, 2026a)

The follow-up public statement of 23 June 2026 hardened the message further: unauthorised CASPs were expected to take immediate steps to wind down EU activities, notify clients, and facilitate transfer of assets either to an authorised CASP or to a self-hosted wallet. ESMA and national competent authorities (NCAs) also signaled coordinated cross-border action. (ESMA, 2026b)

The EBA issued its Travel Rule Guidelines on 4 July 2024 because the regulation itself did not specify all information fields in sufficient detail and could otherwise have produced divergent interpretations and unnecessary rejection of compliant transfers. In other words, the regulatory change was not only legal but also technical: CASPs had to redesign messaging, data validation, and exception handling. (EBA, 2024)

EU CASPs must obtain and hold the self-hosted address, ensure that each transfer can be individually identified, and assess whether the address is owned or controlled by the customer when the transfer exceeds EUR 1,000. These duties are separate from the zero-threshold rule: all transfers are in scope for Travel Rule purposes, but transfers above EUR 1,000 to or from self-hosted wallets trigger extra ownership/control checks. (EBA, 2024)

This matters commercially. Firms that built for basic screening but not wallet verification, attribution, recordkeeping, and transfer-by-transfer identification face operational non-compliance, even if they already have MiCA ambitions. That is why several 2026 compliance analyses describe MiCA, TFR, and AML obligations as a single compliance surface rather than three separate workstreams. (Zyphe, 2026)

ESMA’s reverse-solicitation guidelines, published on 26 February 2025 and applying 60 calendar days after publication in all EU languages, substantially narrowed the practical ability of third-country firms to serve EU clients without authorisation. ESMA states that solicitation must be construed broadly and in a technology-neutral manner. It includes promotion, advertisement, or offers through websites, apps, social media, emails, banners, pop-ups, road shows, affiliation campaigns, retargeting, messaging platforms, and sponsorship deals. Even general brand advertising with broad public reach may count. (ESMA, 2025a)

Once the MiCA transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, reverse solicitation stopped being a peripheral legal theory and became the last narrow exception for unlicensed non-EU firms. ESMA’s April and June 2026 statements linked reverse-solicitation abuse directly to coordinated supervisory action and wind-down expectations. (ESMA, 2026a; ESMA, 2026b)

A persistent market misunderstanding was that 1 July 2026 marked the start of European stablecoin regulation. It did not. The stablecoin provisions for asset-referenced tokens (ARTs) and e-money tokens (EMTs) became applicable on 30 June 2024. The July 2026 date mainly ended grandfathering for CASPs. (InnReg, 2026; 0xProcessing, 2026)

The EBA’s 2025 opinion is one of the most important deeper regulatory developments. EMTs have a dual legal nature: under MiCA they are crypto-assets, but MiCA Article 48(2) also deems them electronic money, meaning they are treated as “funds” for PSD2 purposes. This creates a genuine overlap between crypto regulation and payment regulation. (EBA, 2025)

MiCA is a residual regime, not a universal one. If a token qualifies as a financial instrument under MiFID II, it falls outside MiCA’s crypto-asset perimeter and into the existing securities regime. ESMA’s 19 March 2025 guidelines were designed to improve common, consistent assessment of when crypto-assets should qualify as financial instruments. (ESMA, 2025c)
